Surat al-Qadr (The Night of Decree)

Al-Suyuti said: "There are two opinions about it. The majority view is that it is Meccan, and its verses number five."

[p. 6219]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

[1–5] ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord for every matter.﴾ ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn.﴾

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾: that is, We sent down the Qur'an upon the heart of the Seal of the Prophets, meaning that We began its revelation during the Night of Decree. It has been described as blessed in His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night. Indeed, We were ever warning.﴾ [44:3] It was in Ramadan, according to His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed as guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and criterion.﴾ [2:185]

The Imam said: It was named the Night of Decree either in the sense of the Night of Determination, because God, the Exalted, began therein the determination of His religion and the outlining of the plan for His Prophet in calling people to that which would rescue them from what they were in; or in the sense of greatness and nobility, from the expression "so-and-so has a qadr," meaning he has honour and greatness, because God elevated therein the station of His Prophet and honoured him and magnified him with prophethood. He has come with that which contains an indication, indeed an explicit statement, that it is a glorious night, by the majesty of what took place in it of the sending down of the Qur'an. So He said: ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [97:2] That is: what is it that informs you of the extent of its status and the eminence of its affair?

﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ [97:3] So He repeated its mention three times. Then He used the interrogative, which indicates (p. 6220) that its nobility is not something whose full knowledge is easily grasped. Then He said: "It is better than a thousand months," because thousands of months had passed over the nations while they were groping in the darkness of misguidance; so a night in which the light of guidance shines forth is better than a thousand months of their earlier months. You may pause at the text regarding the preference, and leave to God, the Exalted, the determination of that to which the night is preferred by a thousand months, for He is the One who knows the reason for that and has not explained it to us. You may also take the speech according to their customary way of addressing one another. This is frequent in the Book, and among it is the interrogative occurring in these sūrahs: ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾, for it follows their customary manner of address; otherwise, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, does not ask about anything. So the specification by a thousand has no implicit restriction (mafhūm); rather the purpose of it is to indicate abundance, and the least number that it surpasses is a thousand months. Then the degrees of its excellence over this number are not limited. Thus, when you say: "Concealing charity is better than displaying it," you do not specify the degree of superiority, and there are degrees upon degrees. In the Book, in one single event, the Battle of Badr, God reinforced the believers with a thousand angels, or with three thousand, or with five thousand, as you see in al-Anfal and Āl ʿImrān. There the number has no implicit restriction, as is evident. So it is a night better than a lifetime, God willing.

Then He resumed to explain some of its merits, saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [97:4]. He, may His majesty be exalted, informs that the first occasion of the Prophet (ﷺ) witnessing the angels was on that night. They descended from their spiritual world, which no limit confines and no measure encompasses, until they appeared to his sight (ﷺ). The Spirit is the one who appeared to him as a conveyer of revelation, and he is the one named in the Qur'an as Jibril (Gabriel). The angels and the Spirit only manifest ﴿by permission of their Lord﴾ [97:4], that is: the angels only become manifest to the perfected soul, after God has prepared it to receive their manifestation. The angels do not manifest to all souls, as is well known; that is the grace of God, which He bestows upon whomever He wills. His bestowal of it is His permission and His will. Furthermore, this permission originates in commands and rulings, because God makes the angels manifest to souls in order to convey what He wills from them. Therefore He said: ﴿for every matter﴾ [97:4], that is: God manifests the angels and the Spirit to His messengers at every matter He wishes to communicate to His servants, so the permission in this sense begins from the command.

(p. 6221) The "matter" here is the matter in His words: ﴿Therein is made distinct every wise matter﴾ [44:4], ﴿a command from Us; indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ [44:5]. So the discourse concerns the message, the commands and the rulings, and nothing beyond them. For this reason some have said that "min" (from) here means "bi" (with), that is: "with every matter." There is no need for that, given what we have said. He used the present tense in His words ﴿The angels descend﴾ [97:4] and His words ﴿Therein is made distinct every wise matter﴾ [44:4], even though the meaning is past, for two reasons, since the discussion concerns the beginning of the Qur'an's descent:

The first: to make the past present in the mind because of its greatness, as in His words: ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger said﴾ [2:214], for the present tense after the past adds vividness to the depiction.

The second: because the beginning of the descent occurred therein, but the rest of the Book and what it contains of detailed commands and rulings came afterwards. It is as if He is indicating that what began therein continues into the future until it completes the religion. His, the Exalted's, words ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾ [97:5] mean that it was a night free from every evil and harm. Describing it as peace itself, which is safety and security, is for emphasis that no turbidity mixed with it, but rather God relieved His Prophet of every distress therein and opened for him therein the paths of guidance, and thereby granted him what he had been longing for over long days and months.

Notes:

First: We have mentioned that the Night of Decree in which the revelation of the Qur'an began was in Ramadan, according to the verse ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [2:185]. There is no consensus on determining that night. Rather, in Sahih al-Bukhari it is reported that it "was lifted," that is, knowledge of its specific identification was lifted. In another narration in it: "I forgot it or I was made to forget it," from the words of the one upon whom be the blessings of God. For this reason he encouraged standing in prayer throughout the whole of Ramadan, hoping to coincide with it on one of its nights. Indeed, the narration with stronger chains holds that it is in "the last ten [nights] of Ramadan," because of his (ﷺ) great concern with seclusion in it, reviving its nights and waking his family. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan and Qatadah held that it is the night of the twenty-fourth.

(p. 6222) Ibn Hajar said: Their evidence is the hadith of Wathilah: "The Qur'an was revealed on the twenty-fourth of Ramadan." The sayings of the early generations (salaf) about it, companions and those after them, have varied so much that they have reached over forty opinions.

The Imam said: Then the sound reports are consistent that it is in the month of Ramadan, but we do not specify it among its nights. The narrations have differed greatly concerning it, and the Book of God did not specify it. What has been reported in the hadiths about mentioning it was intended only to urge believers to revive it with worship, in gratitude to God, the Exalted, for having guided them to this religion whose outpouring He began among them within its span. They may worship God during it, individually and collectively. Whoever finds a report more convincing for a night, let him revive it, and whoever wishes to coincide with it with certainty, let him thank God by devoting himself to acts of worship throughout the whole month. This is the secret of its not being specified. The verse of al-Baqarah points to it, for it makes the whole month a container for the descent of the Qur'an, so that believers may remember God's blessing upon them therein. So it is a night of worship and humility and remembrance of the blessing of truth and religion. It should not be a night of boasting and frivolity, in which the mosques of God are made into arenas for show-off, where hypocrites race to attend and sincere ones wish to stay away from it, as the practice of Muslims has been in these days. Indeed, all that they have retained of the Night of Decree is that they have a period of evening gathering in which they talk about what God does not look upon, and hear some of the Book of God without contemplating its meaning or taking lessons from its meanings. Rather, if they listen to it at all, they listen only to the melody of the reciter. Then they hear from sayings whose reports are not authentic and whose effects are not praised among the later or earlier generations. They also have fancies about the Night of Decree that are unworthy even of the minds of children, let alone of mature men. End of quotation.

Al-Tabari said: The concealment of the Night of Decree is a proof of the falsehood of whoever claims that in that night there appears to the eyes what does not appear during the rest of the year; for if that were true, it would not have been hidden from everyone who stood in prayer through the nights of the year, let alone the nights of Ramadan.

Second: Ibn Hajar, in Fath al-Bari, related an opinion from some scholars that the Night of Decree was specific to one year that occurred during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). Perhaps its basis is the authentic report that it "was lifted," the meaning of which we have already mentioned; for this reason the majority held otherwise. In my view there is no contradiction, because what is meant by the first is the night of the descent of the Qur'an and the particular manifestation that occurred in it, which was unique to it; and by the second is that the night in Ramadan corresponding to it every year is a night having a distinction over others, by a grace specific to it alone. This is the secret of standing in prayer during Ramadan and seeking it in the last ten [nights] of it, namely reviving the nights that resemble it, seeking blessing, and giving thanks to God, the Exalted, for that blessing and guidance. So whoever stands in the last ten nights, or in Ramadan, certainly coincides with what resembles that night, because it is definitely within it. Islam has differed in preferring certain times by legislating them as seasons of worship from what the leaders of other religions invented in their commemorations, making them festivals, whose hours are spent in idleness, adornment and amusement, which contradicts the wisdom of their remembrance. So consider the difference and praise God for following the truth.

Third: The Imam said: What many people say, that the blessed night in which every wise matter is distinguished is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and that the matters distinguished therein are provisions and lifespans, and likewise what they say of the like of that concerning the Night of Decree, is an audacity of speaking about the unseen without a decisive proof. It is not permissible for us to hold any belief in any of that unless a mutawatir (widely transmitted) report from the infallible one (ﷺ) has come concerning it, and no such report has come, because of the inconsistency of the narrations, the weakness of most of them, and the falsehood of many of them. Such things cannot validly be adopted in matters of creed. The same is said of Bayt al-ʿIzza (the House of Majesty) and of the Qur'an's descent therein all at once on that night, for it is not permissible to include it among the articles of religion, since its report is not mutawatir from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is not permissible for us to rely on conjecture in a creed like this, lest we be among those of whom "they follow nothing but conjecture" [53:23]; we seek refuge in God. Muslims have fallen into this calamity, the calamity of confusing what may validly be believed of God's unseen and counted among the articles of religion, with what is merely supposed in order to act upon some virtue of virtues. So beware of falling into it as they did. End of his words, may God, the Exalted, have mercy on him.

Third: The Imam said: What many people say, that the blessed night in which every wise matter is distinguished is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and that the matters distinguished therein are provisions and lifespans, and likewise what they say of the like of that concerning the Night of Decree, is an audacity of speaking about the unseen without a decisive proof. It is not permissible for us to hold any belief in any of that unless a mutawatir (widely transmitted) report from the infallible one (ﷺ) has come concerning it, and no such report has come, because of the inconsistency of the narrations, the weakness of most of them, and the falsehood of many of them. Such things cannot validly be adopted in matters of creed. The same is said of Bayt al-ʿIzza (the House of Majesty) and of the Qur'an's descent therein all at once on that night, for it is not permissible to include it among the articles of religion, since its report is not mutawatir from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is not permissible for us to rely on conjecture in a creed like this, lest we be among those of whom "they follow nothing but conjecture" [53:23]; we seek refuge in God. Muslims have fallen into this calamity, the calamity of confusing what may validly be believed of God's unseen and counted among the articles of religion, with what is merely supposed in order to act upon some virtue of virtues. So beware of falling into it as they did. End of his words, may God, the Exalted, have mercy on him.
